notes.front: What is a reusable workflow?
notes.back: A workflow that you, and anyone with access to it, can call from another workflow instead of copying and pasting it.
notes.explanation: One shared workflow is called from other workflows, rather than each of them carrying its own copy.
notes.example: Like a recipe card pinned up in a shared kitchen: each cook follows the same card instead of keeping a private copy.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Rather than copying and pasting from one workflow to another, you can make workflows reusable. You and anyone with access to the reusable workflow can then call the reusable workflow from another workflow.

notes.front: What is a caller workflow?
notes.back: A workflow that uses another workflow; one caller workflow can use several reusable workflows.
notes.explanation: The caller is the workflow doing the calling, as opposed to the reusable workflow it calls.
notes.example: Like a project manager's plan that names which specialist does each part of the work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: A workflow that uses another workflow is referred to as a "caller" workflow. The reusable workflow is a "called" workflow. One caller workflow can use multiple called workflows.

notes.front: What is a called workflow?
notes.back: The reusable workflow that a caller workflow uses; the whole of it runs as if it were part of the caller.
notes.explanation: Each called workflow is referenced in a single line, yet the entire called workflow is used when the caller runs.
notes.example: Like a subcontractor on a building job: brought in by name, and doing their whole trade inside your project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Each called workflow is referenced in a single line. The result is that the caller workflow file may contain just a few lines of YAML, but may perform a large number of tasks when it's run. When you reuse a workflow, the entire called workflow is used, just as if it was part of the caller workflow.

notes.front: What does `secrets: inherit` do in a job that calls a reusable workflow?
notes.back: It passes all the calling workflow's secrets to the called workflow.
notes.explanation: That means every secret the caller can access, namely organisation, repository and environment secrets.
notes.example: Like handing a locum doctor the practice's whole key ring instead of the one key they asked for.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions”, “`jobs.<job_id>.secrets.inherit`”
notes.evidence: Use the `inherit` keyword to pass all the calling workflow's secrets to the called workflow. This includes all secrets the calling workflow has access to, namely organization, repository, and environment secrets.

notes.front: What is a workflow template?
notes.back: A starting point you choose when creating a new workflow, which does some or all of the work of writing it.
notes.explanation: It lets people in the organisation who may create workflows do so more quickly and easily.
notes.example: Like a form letter with blanks: you start from it, fill in your details and send your own copy.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Workflow templates”
notes.evidence: Workflow templates allow everyone in your organization who has permission to create workflows to do so more quickly and easily. When people create a new workflow, they can choose a workflow template and some or all of the work of writing the workflow will be done for them.

notes.front: In the exam study guide, what are "starter workflows"?
notes.back: Workflow templates: a scaffold copied into a new workflow, which is independent of the template once created.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs call these workflow templates; the study guide calls them starter workflows, public or organisation-only, and contrasts them with reusable workflows.
notes.example: Like a flat-pack starter kit: once you have built your shelf from it, changes to the kit's instructions do not reach your shelf.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Study guide for Exam GH-200: GitHub Actions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where do an organisation's own workflow templates live?
notes.back: In a repository named `.github` in the organisation, inside its `workflow-templates` directory.
notes.explanation: You create the `.github` repository if it does not already exist, then add the template files to `workflow-templates`.
notes.example: Like a shared "templates" folder on an office drive: one agreed place that everyone's New menu reads from.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating workflow templates for your organization”, “Creating workflow templates”
notes.evidence: If it doesn't already exist, create a new repository named `.github` in your organization. 2. Create a directory named `workflow-templates`. 3. Create your new workflow file inside the `workflow-templates` directory.

notes.front: What does the `$default-branch` placeholder do in a workflow template?
notes.back: When a workflow is created from the template, it is replaced with the name of the repository's default branch.
notes.explanation: A template can refer to the default branch without knowing what each repository calls it.
notes.example: Like a mail-merge field such as «FirstName»: written once in the template, filled in for each copy.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “The `$default-branch` placeholder”
notes.evidence: If you need to refer to a repository's default branch, you can use the `$default-branch` placeholder in your workflow template. When a workflow is created the placeholder will be automatically replaced with the name of the repository's default branch.

notes.front: Where must a reusable workflow file be stored?
notes.back: In the repository's `.github/workflows` directory; subdirectories of `workflows` are not supported.
notes.explanation: Reusable workflows live where any other workflow file lives, and not in a folder beneath it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Creating a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: As with other workflow files, you locate reusable workflows in the `.github/workflows` directory of a repository. Subdirectories of the `workflows` directory are not supported.

notes.front: For a workflow to be reusable, its `on` values must include {{c1::`workflow_call`}}.
notes.back: `workflow_call`
notes.explanation: This is the event that lets another workflow call it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Creating a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: For a workflow to be reusable, the values for `on` must include `workflow_call`:

notes.front: Where in a caller workflow do you call a reusable workflow?
notes.back: Directly within a job, with `uses`, not from within the job's steps.
notes.explanation: This differs from actions, which you use from within steps.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Calling a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: You call a reusable workflow by using the `uses` keyword. Unlike when you are using actions within a workflow, you call reusable workflows directly within a job, and not from within job steps.

notes.front: A reusable workflow in another repository is referenced as {{c1::`{owner}/{repo}/.github/workflows/{filename}@{ref}`}}.
notes.back: `{owner}/{repo}/.github/workflows/{filename}@{ref}`
notes.explanation: This form works for reusable workflows in public and private repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Calling a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: `{owner}/{repo}/.github/workflows/{filename}@{ref}` for reusable workflows in public and private repositories.

notes.front: When you call a reusable workflow as `{owner}/{repo}/…@{ref}`, what can `{ref}` be?
notes.back: A commit `SHA`, a release tag or a branch name.
notes.explanation: The docs call the commit `SHA` the safest option for stability and security, and a release tag wins over a branch of the same name.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Calling a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: When you reference a reusable workflow with `{owner}/{repo}` and `@{ref}`, the `{ref}` can be a SHA, a release tag, or a branch name. If a release tag and a branch have the same name, the release tag takes precedence over the branch name. Using the commit SHA is the safest option for stability and security.

notes.front: You call a reusable workflow in the same repository as `./.github/workflows/{filename}`. From which commit does the called workflow come?
notes.back: From the same commit as the caller workflow.
notes.explanation: A local reference has no `{owner}/{repo}` and no `@{ref}`, so it follows the caller's own commit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Calling a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: When you reference a reusable workflow in the same repository using `$/` or `./` (without `{owner}/{repo}` and `@{ref}`), the called workflow is from the same commit as the caller workflow.

notes.front: In a job's `uses` value for a reusable workflow, may you use an expression, or a `refs/heads/` prefix?
notes.back: No: contexts and expressions are not allowed, and nor are ref prefixes such as `refs/heads` and `refs/tags`.
notes.explanation: The reference must be written out literally.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Calling a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: Ref prefixes such as `refs/heads` and `refs/tags` are not allowed. You cannot use contexts or expressions in this keyword.

notes.front: In the reusable workflow, where do you define the inputs and secrets that a caller will pass?
notes.back: Under `on.workflow_call`, with the `inputs` and `secrets` keywords.
notes.explanation: The reusable workflow then references what it defined there.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using inputs and secrets in a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: In the reusable workflow, use the `inputs` and `secrets` keywords to define inputs or secrets that will be passed from a caller workflow.

notes.front: In a calling job, which keywords pass named inputs and named secrets to a reusable workflow?
notes.back: `with` for inputs; `secrets` for secrets.
notes.explanation: A reusable workflow is called from a job, so both keywords go on the calling job beside its `uses` line: `with` carries input values and `secrets` carries named secrets.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Passing inputs and secrets to a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: To pass named inputs to a called workflow, use the `with` keyword in a job. Use the `secrets` keyword to pass named secrets.

notes.front: An input passed to a called workflow must match the type it declares: boolean, number or {{c1::string}}.
notes.back: string
notes.explanation: The value's data type must match the one specified in the called workflow.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Passing inputs and secrets to a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: To pass named inputs to a called workflow, use the `with` keyword in a job. Use the `secrets` keyword to pass named secrets. For inputs, the data type of the input value must match the type specified in the called workflow (either boolean, number, or string).

notes.front: Can a caller workflow pass environment secrets to a reusable workflow?
notes.back: No: `on.workflow_call` does not support the `environment` keyword.
notes.explanation: If the reusable workflow sets `environment` on a job, that environment's secret is used, not the one passed by the caller.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using inputs and secrets in a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: Environment secrets cannot be passed from the caller workflow as `on.workflow_call` does not support the `environment` keyword. If you include `environment` in the reusable workflow at the job level, the environment secret will be used, and not the secret passed from the caller workflow.

notes.front: Must secrets passed with `secrets: inherit` be declared in the called workflow's `on` key?
notes.back: No: inherited secrets can be referenced even if they are not explicitly defined there.
notes.explanation: Only secrets passed one by one need declaring under `on.workflow_call`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using inputs and secrets in a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: If the secrets are inherited by using `secrets: inherit` in the calling workflow, you can reference them even if they are not explicitly defined in the `on` key.

notes.front: Across which boundaries can `secrets: inherit` pass secrets?
notes.back: Across repositories in the same organisation, or across organisations in the same enterprise.
notes.explanation: The limit is the enterprise: inheriting does not reach beyond it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions”, “`jobs.<job_id>.secrets.inherit`”
notes.evidence: The `inherit` keyword can be used to pass secrets across repositories within the same organization, or across organizations within the same enterprise.

notes.front: In a chain of workflows A > B > C, when does C receive a secret that A holds?
notes.back: Only if A passes it to B, and B then passes it to C.
notes.explanation: Secrets go only to the directly called workflow, so each link in the chain must pass them on.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Passing secrets to nested workflows”
notes.evidence: Secrets are only passed to directly called workflow, so in the workflow chain A > B > C, workflow C will only receive secrets from A if they have been passed from A to B, and then from B to C.

notes.front: A reusable workflow produces data the caller needs. What must the reusable workflow do?
notes.back: Specify that data as outputs of the reusable workflow.
notes.explanation: Only declared outputs are available to the caller workflow.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using outputs from a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: A reusable workflow may generate data that you want to use in the caller workflow. To use these outputs, you must specify them as the outputs of the reusable workflow.

notes.front: In a reusable workflow's outputs, what must each output's `value` point to?
notes.back: A job-level output of the called workflow; step outputs must first be mapped to job outputs.
notes.explanation: The chain runs from step output to job output to workflow output.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using outputs from a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: The `value` must be set to the value of a job-level output within the called workflow. Step-level outputs must first be mapped to job-level outputs as shown below.

notes.front: A reusable workflow that sets an output is run with a matrix strategy. Which value reaches the caller?
notes.back: The output of the last successfully completing run of the matrix that actually set a value.
notes.explanation: A later run that set an empty string does not count as having set a value.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using outputs from a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: If a reusable workflow that sets an output is executed with a matrix strategy, the output will be the output set by the last successful completing reusable workflow of the matrix which actually sets a value.

notes.front: How can a matrix strategy help when calling a reusable workflow?
notes.back: It creates one job run per combination of its variables, for example to pass different inputs to the reusable workflow.
notes.explanation: The calling job defines the matrix and passes `matrix` values through `with`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using a matrix strategy with a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: A matrix strategy lets you use variables in a single job definition to automatically create multiple job runs that are based on the combinations of the variables. For example, you can use a matrix strategy to pass different inputs to a reusable workflow.

notes.front: Can a job that calls a reusable workflow use any job keyword it likes?
notes.back: No: only a fixed list, such as `name`, `uses`, `with`, `secrets`, `strategy`, `needs` and `if`.
notes.explanation: Other job keywords, such as `runs-on` and `steps`, are not on that list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Supported keywords for jobs that call a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: When you call a reusable workflow, you can only use the following keywords in the job containing the call: jobs.<job_id>.name jobs.<job_id>.uses jobs.<job_id>.with

notes.front: In which three cases can a workflow use a reusable workflow?
notes.back: Same repository; called workflow in a public repository the organisation allows; or in a private repository whose settings allow access.
notes.explanation: Any one of the three is enough.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Access to reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: A reusable workflow can be used by another workflow if any of the following is true: Both workflows are in the same repository. The called workflow is stored in a public repository, and your organization allows you to use public reusable workflows.

notes.front: A caller in a `private` repository can use reusable workflows from `private` and `public` repositories; a caller in a `public` repository, only from {{c1::`public`}} ones.
notes.back: `public`
notes.explanation: A caller in a private repository reaches both kinds.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Access to reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: `private` | `private` and `public`

notes.front: For a reusable workflow in a private repository, what must be set on that repository?
notes.back: Its Actions settings Access policy must explicitly allow access from the repositories that contain the caller workflows.
notes.explanation: Being in the same organisation is not enough on its own; the called workflow's repository must opt in.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Access to reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: For private repositories, the Access policy on the Actions settings page of the called workflow's repository must be explicitly configured to allow access from repositories containing caller workflows

notes.front: You can connect at most {{c1::ten}} levels of workflows: the top-level caller workflow and up to nine levels of reusable workflows.
notes.back: ten
notes.explanation: The count includes the top-level caller itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Nesting reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: You can connect a maximum of ten levels of workflows - that is, the top-level caller workflow and up to nine levels of reusable workflows.

notes.front: A single workflow file can call at most {{c1::50}} unique reusable workflows, counting any nested trees it calls.
notes.explanation: Workflows reached through nesting count towards the same limit as those called directly.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Limitations of reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: You can call a maximum of 50 unique reusable workflows from a single workflow file. This limit includes any trees of nested reusable workflows that may be called starting from your top-level caller workflow file.

notes.front: Does a workflow-level `env` in the caller workflow reach the called workflow?
notes.back: No: environment variables in the caller's workflow-level `env` context are not propagated to the called workflow.
notes.explanation: Pass what the called workflow needs as inputs, or use the `vars` context for shared variables.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Limitations of reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Any environment variables set in an `env` context defined at the workflow level in the caller workflow are not propagated to the called workflow.

notes.front: How does a caller get a value that the called workflow set in its `env` context?
notes.back: Not through `env`: it is not accessible to the caller, so the called workflow must return it as an output.
notes.explanation: Environment variables do not cross the boundary in either direction.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Limitations of reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Similarly, environment variables set in the `env` context, defined in the called workflow, are not accessible in the `env` context of the caller workflow. Instead, you must use outputs of the reusable workflow.

notes.front: Why can't a reusable workflow use `GITHUB_ENV` to pass values to job steps in the caller workflow?
notes.back: Because reusable workflows are called directly within a job, not from within a job step.
notes.explanation: There is no step in the caller's job for the value to reach.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Limitations of reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Reusable workflows are called directly within a job, and not from within a job step. You cannot, therefore, use `GITHUB_ENV` to pass values to job steps in the caller workflow.

notes.front: In nested reusable workflows, how can `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions change down the chain?
notes.back: They can only stay the same or become more restrictive, never more permissive.
notes.explanation: If the top workflow has only read permission for something, the workflows it calls cannot have write permission for it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Access and permissions for nested workflows”
notes.evidence: `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions can only be the same or more restrictive in nested workflows. For example, in the workflow chain A > B > C, if workflow A has `package: read` token permission, then B and C cannot have `package: write` permission.

notes.front: Caller and called workflows both use `${{ github.workflow }}` as their concurrency group, with `cancel-in-progress: true`. What happens?
notes.back: The caller workflow is cancelled when the called workflow runs.
notes.explanation: A called workflow uses its caller's name in `github.workflow`, so both land in the same group.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Supported keywords for jobs that call a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: A called workflow uses the name of its caller workflow in ${{ github.workflow }}, so using this context as the value of `jobs.<job_id>.concurrency.group` in both caller and called workflows will cause the caller workflow to be cancelled when the called workflow runs.

notes.front: For GitHub-hosted runners, whose context decides runner assignment for a reusable workflow, and who is billed?
notes.back: The caller's, in both cases.
notes.explanation: The caller workflow cannot use GitHub-hosted runners from the called workflow's repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “How reusable workflows use runners”
notes.evidence: The assignment of GitHub-hosted runners is always evaluated using only the caller's context. Billing for GitHub-hosted runners is always associated with the caller. The caller workflow cannot use GitHub-hosted runners from the called repository.

notes.front: When a caller workflow triggers a reusable workflow, which workflow is the `github` context associated with?
notes.back: Always the caller workflow.
notes.explanation: The called workflow is also automatically granted access to `github.token` and `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “`github` context”
notes.evidence: When a reusable workflow is triggered by a caller workflow, the `github` context is always associated with the caller workflow. The called workflow is automatically granted access to `github.token` and `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN`.

notes.front: A called workflow from another repository runs `actions/checkout`. Whose contents does it check out?
notes.back: The repository that hosts the caller workflow, not the called workflow's.
notes.explanation: Actions in a called workflow run as if they were part of the caller workflow.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: If you reuse a workflow from a different repository, any actions in the called workflow run as if they were part of the caller workflow. For example, if the called workflow uses `actions/checkout`, the action checks out the contents of the repository that hosts the caller workflow, not the called workflow.

notes.front: How can a workflow template help people benefit from centrally managed workflow code?
notes.back: By referencing reusable workflows inside the template.
notes.explanation: The template gives each new workflow a start, and the reusable workflows it calls stay managed in one place.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Workflow templates”
notes.evidence: Within a workflow template, you can also reference reusable workflows to make it easy for people to benefit from reusing centrally managed workflow code.

notes.front: A template references a reusable workflow. How do you make sure everyone who uses it runs the same code?
notes.back: Reference the reusable workflow by a commit `SHA`; by tag or branch, be sure you can trust that version.
notes.explanation: A commit reference fixes the code for everyone; a tag or branch may point at different code later.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Workflow templates”
notes.evidence: If you use a commit SHA when referencing the reusable workflow, you can ensure that everyone who reuses that workflow will always be using the same YAML code. However, if you reference a reusable workflow by a tag or branch, be sure that you can trust that version of the workflow.

notes.front: When you set up workflows in a repository, how does GitHub choose which workflow templates to recommend?
notes.back: It analyses the repository's code and recommends workflows for its language and framework.
notes.explanation: You can also search and filter to find other relevant templates.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Workflow templates”
notes.evidence: When you set up workflows in your repository, GitHub analyzes the code in your repository and recommends workflows based on the language and framework in your repository.

notes.front: Which category of GitHub's workflow templates covers triaging pull requests and greeting first-time contributors?
notes.back: Automation.
notes.explanation: Automation templates offer ways to automate workflows around the repository, such as labelling pull requests by the paths they change.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Workflow templates”
notes.evidence: Automation workflow templates offer solutions for automating workflows, such as triaging pull requests and applying a label based on the paths that are modified in the pull request, or greeting users who are first time contributors to the repository.

notes.front: You can browse the full list of GitHub's workflow templates in the {{c1::`actions/starter-workflows`}} repository.
notes.back: `actions/starter-workflows`
notes.explanation: You can use these templates as a starting place for your own workflow or as they are.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Workflow templates”
notes.evidence: Use these workflows as a starting place to build your custom workflow or use them as-is. You can browse the full list of workflow templates in the actions/starter-workflows repository.

notes.front: On the "Choose a workflow" page, how do you start from a workflow template?
notes.back: Find it, by keyword search or category filter if needed, then click Configure.
notes.explanation: The page shows a selection of recommended templates first.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow templates”, “Choosing and using a workflow template”
notes.evidence: The "Choose a workflow" page shows a selection of recommended workflow templates. Find the workflow template that you want to use, then click Configure

notes.front: A workflow template refers to a secret. What must you do before it will work?
notes.back: Store the value that the secret name describes as a secret in your repository.
notes.explanation: The template names the secret; the value has to come from your repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow templates”, “Choosing and using a workflow template”
notes.evidence: Some workflow templates use secrets. For example, `${{ secrets.npm_token }}`. If the workflow template uses a secret, store the value described in the secret name as a secret in your repository.

notes.front: In an organisation's `.github` repository, template workflow files go in a directory named {{c1::`workflow-templates`}}.
notes.back: `workflow-templates`
notes.explanation: To add another template, you add its files to the same directory.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating workflow templates for your organization”, “Creating workflow templates”
notes.evidence: If it doesn't already exist, create a new repository named `.github` in your organization. 2. Create a directory named `workflow-templates`. 3. Create your new workflow file inside the `workflow-templates` directory.

notes.front: The metadata file for the template `deploy.yml` must be named {{c1::`deploy.properties.json`}}.
notes.back: `deploy.properties.json`
notes.explanation: It has the same name as the workflow file, with `.properties.json` in place of `.yml`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Metadata file requirements”
notes.evidence: The metadata file must have the same name as the workflow file, but instead of the `.yml` extension, it must be appended with `.properties.json`.

notes.front: Which two fields are required in a workflow template's metadata file?
notes.back: `name` and `description`.
notes.explanation: Both are displayed in the list of available workflows; `iconName`, `categories` and `filePatterns` are optional.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Metadata file requirements”
notes.evidence: `name` - Required. The name of the workflow. This is displayed in the list of available workflows. `description` - Required. The description of the workflow. This is displayed in the list of available workflows.

notes.front: Templates in a public `.github` repository are available to which repositories?
notes.back: All repository types.
notes.explanation: Templates can be used in repositories whose visibility matches or is more restricted than the template repository's.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Workflow template availability”
notes.evidence: You can use templates in repositories that match or have more restricted visibility than the template repository. Workflow templates in a public `.github` repository are available to all repository types.

notes.front: Templates in a private `.github` repository are available to which repositories?
notes.back: Only private repositories.
notes.explanation: A template repository can serve repositories of the same or more restricted visibility, and nothing is more restricted than private.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Workflow template availability”
notes.evidence: Workflow templates in a private `.github` repository are only available to private repositories.

notes.front: Your templates sit in a private or internal `.github` repository. What must you grant, and to whom?
notes.back: Read access, to the users or teams who should be able to use the templates.
notes.explanation: Without it, people cannot use templates from a non-public `.github` repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Granting access for private/internal repositories”
notes.evidence: If you're using a private or internal `.github` repository, you need to grant Read access to users or teams who should be able to use the templates.

notes.front: How do you let other private repositories in your organisation use a reusable workflow kept in a private repository?
notes.back: In that repository's Actions → General settings, under Access, choose "Accessible from repositories in the organisation".
notes.explanation: This shares it within the organisation without publishing it publicly.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”
notes.evidence: To grant access to other private repositories in the organization, in the Access section at the bottom of the page, select Accessible from repositories in the 'ORGANIZATION-NAME' organization

notes.front: Your reusable workflow is in a private repository on your personal account. Which Access option shares it with your other private repositories?
notes.back: "Accessible from repositories owned by" your user.
notes.explanation: It is the personal-account counterpart of the organisation setting.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows from your private repository”, “Sharing actions and workflows from your private repository”
notes.evidence: To grant access to other private repositories, in the Access section at the bottom of the page, select Accessible from repositories owned by 'USERNAME' user

notes.front: You make a private repository's workflows accessible to other repositories. What can outside collaborators on those repositories then see?
notes.back: Logs of workflow runs that use actions or workflows from your private repository.
notes.explanation: They gain this indirect access even without direct access to your private repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”
notes.evidence: If you make a private repository accessible to GitHub Actions workflows in other repositories, outside collaborators on the other repositories can indirectly access the private repository, even though they do not have direct access to these repositories. The outside collaborators can view logs for workflow runs when actions or workflows from the private repository are used.

notes.front: To let runners download shared private actions, GitHub passes a scoped token to the runner. What access does it have, and when does it expire?
notes.back: Read access to the repository; it expires automatically after one hour.
notes.explanation: The token is limited in both scope and lifetime.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”
notes.evidence: To allow runners to download these actions, GitHub passes a scoped installation token to the runner. This token has read access to the repository, and automatically expires after one hour.

notes.front: You save a reusable workflow as `.github/workflows/shared/deploy.yml`, and callers cannot use it. What is wrong?
notes.choices:
A) Subdirectories of `workflows` are not supported
B) It must be in a repository named `.github`
C) Reusable workflows must be public
D) It needs `on: workflow_dispatch`
notes.back: A) Subdirectories of `workflows` are not supported
notes.choicesExplained: D: a reusable workflow needs `workflow_call`. B: that is where organisation templates live, not reusable workflows. C: private reusable workflows can be shared too.
notes.explanation: Reusable workflows go directly in `.github/workflows`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Creating a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: As with other workflow files, you locate reusable workflows in the `.github/workflows` directory of a repository. Subdirectories of the `workflows` directory are not supported.

notes.front: A job has `runs-on` and `steps`, and one step says `uses: my-org/ci/.github/workflows/test.yml@v1`. It fails. What is the fix?
notes.choices:
A) Change `@v1` to `@main`
B) Add `with:` to the step
C) Move the `uses` line to the job level, as its own job
D) Add `secrets: inherit` to the step
notes.back: C) Move the `uses` line to the job level, as its own job
notes.choicesExplained: B, A and D: none of these changes where the call is made; a reusable workflow is never called from a step.
notes.explanation: Reusable workflows are called directly within a job, not from within job steps.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Calling a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: You call a reusable workflow by using the `uses` keyword. Unlike when you are using actions within a workflow, you call reusable workflows directly within a job, and not from within job steps.

notes.front: Your repository's build workflow calls a lint workflow stored in the same repository. You want the lint workflow taken from the same commit as the caller. How do you reference it?
notes.back: C) `./.github/workflows/lint.yml`
notes.choicesExplained: A: `@main` follows the branch, not the caller's commit. B: expressions are not allowed in `uses`. D: ref prefixes are not allowed.
notes.explanation: A local `./` reference without owner, repository or ref uses the caller's own commit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Calling a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: When you reference a reusable workflow in the same repository using `$/` or `./` (without `{owner}/{repo}` and `@{ref}`), the called workflow is from the same commit as the caller workflow.

notes.front: A called workflow declares `dry-run` as a boolean input. The caller passes `dry-run: "maybe"` under `with`. What goes wrong?
notes.choices:
A) The input's type does not match the boolean the called workflow declares
B) The value is ignored and `false` is used
C) Nothing: inputs are always converted to strings
D) The input must be passed under `secrets` instead
notes.back: A) The input's type does not match the boolean the called workflow declares
notes.choicesExplained: C and B: the docs require the value's type to match, not convert or ignore it. D: `secrets` is for secrets, not ordinary inputs.
notes.explanation: An input value's data type must match the type specified in the called workflow.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Passing inputs and secrets to a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: To pass named inputs to a called workflow, use the `with` keyword in a job. Use the `secrets` keyword to pass named secrets. For inputs, the data type of the input value must match the type specified in the called workflow (either boolean, number, or string).

notes.front: Workflow A calls B with `secrets: inherit`. B calls C passing only `deploy-key`. C also needs A's `registry-token`. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) C receives it, because A used `inherit`
B) C cannot see it, because B did not pass it on
C) C receives every organisation secret automatically
D) C receives it only if C is in the same repository as A
notes.back: B) C cannot see it, because B did not pass it on
notes.choicesExplained: A: inheriting reaches only the directly called workflow, B. C: nothing passes secrets past B automatically. D: the repository does not matter; each link must pass the secret.
notes.explanation: Secrets go only to the directly called workflow, so B must pass `registry-token` to C.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Passing secrets to nested workflows”
notes.evidence: Secrets are only passed to directly called workflow, so in the workflow chain A > B > C, workflow C will only receive secrets from A if they have been passed from A to B, and then from B to C.

notes.front: A caller uses `secrets: inherit` to call a reusable workflow owned by an organisation in a different enterprise. What should you expect?
notes.choices:
A) It works, because `inherit` passes secrets anywhere
B) It does not pass the secrets: `inherit` works within one organisation or across organisations in the same enterprise
C) It works only if the reusable workflow is public
D) It works only for repository secrets
notes.back: B) It does not pass the secrets: `inherit` works within one organisation or across organisations in the same enterprise
notes.choicesExplained: A: `inherit` is limited to the organisation or the enterprise. D: it has no such partial mode. C: visibility controls whether you can call the workflow, not how far secrets are inherited.
notes.explanation: The docs describe inheriting across repositories in one organisation or across organisations in one enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions”, “`jobs.<job_id>.secrets.inherit`”
notes.evidence: The `inherit` keyword can be used to pass secrets across repositories within the same organization, or across organizations within the same enterprise.

notes.front: A reusable workflow computes a version number in a step. A later job in the caller needs it. What must the reusable workflow do?
notes.choices:
A) Write it to `GITHUB_ENV`
B) Set it in its workflow-level `env`
C) Nothing: callers can read any step output directly
D) Map the step output to a job output, then to an output under `on.workflow_call.outputs`
notes.back: D) Map the step output to a job output, then to an output under `on.workflow_call.outputs`
notes.choicesExplained: A: `GITHUB_ENV` cannot reach the caller's steps. B: the called workflow's `env` is not accessible to the caller. C: only declared workflow outputs reach the caller.
notes.explanation: The workflow output's `value` must be a job-level output, and step outputs must first be mapped to job outputs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Using outputs from a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: The `value` must be set to the value of a job-level output within the called workflow. Step-level outputs must first be mapped to job-level outputs as shown below.

notes.front: A workflow in a public repository tries to call a reusable workflow stored in a private repository of the same organisation. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) It works if the caller uses `secrets: inherit`
B) It cannot: a public caller can use only reusable workflows in public repositories
C) It works if the caller pins a commit
D) It works because both are in the same organisation
notes.back: B) It cannot: a public caller can use only reusable workflows in public repositories
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: secrets and pinning do not change which repositories a caller can reach. D: the visibility table allows public callers only public reusable workflows.
notes.explanation: A caller in a private repository can reach private and public reusable workflows; a public one only public ones.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Access to reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: `private` | `private` and `public`

notes.front: A top-level caller starts a chain in which each reusable workflow calls the next, eleven workflows in all. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) It runs, because only 50 unique workflows are counted
B) It runs if every link uses `secrets: inherit`
C) It runs, but only the first ten are logged
D) It exceeds the limit of ten levels, the caller plus nine reusable workflows
notes.back: D) It exceeds the limit of ten levels, the caller plus nine reusable workflows
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 50-workflow limit is separate from the ten-level depth limit. C: there is no partial running. B: secrets do not affect nesting depth.
notes.explanation: Nesting allows at most ten levels, counting the top-level caller.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reuse workflows”, “Nesting reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: You can connect a maximum of ten levels of workflows - that is, the top-level caller workflow and up to nine levels of reusable workflows.

notes.front: A monorepo's main workflow calls 40 different reusable workflows directly, and those call 15 further different ones. What limit does this break?
notes.choices:
A) The limit of 50 unique reusable workflows per workflow file, which includes nested trees
B) None: only direct calls count
C) The ten-level nesting limit
D) The 50 re-runs limit
notes.back: A) The limit of 50 unique reusable workflows per workflow file, which includes nested trees
notes.choicesExplained: C: the chain here is only three levels deep. B: nested workflows count too. D: that limit is about re-runs, not calls.
notes.explanation: Forty plus fifteen makes 55 unique reusable workflows, and nested trees count towards the 50.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Limitations of reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: You can call a maximum of 50 unique reusable workflows from a single workflow file. This limit includes any trees of nested reusable workflows that may be called starting from your top-level caller workflow file.

notes.front: A caller's workflow-level `env` sets `REGION` to `eu-west`. The called workflow reads `env.REGION` and finds it empty. What is the right fix?
notes.choices:
A) Move `env` into the calling job
B) Pass the region as an input with `with`
C) Set `REGION` in `GITHUB_ENV` in the caller
D) Use `secrets: inherit`
notes.back: B) Pass the region as an input with `with`
notes.choicesExplained: A: the calling job cannot hold `env`, and caller environment variables are not propagated anyway. D: that passes secrets, not environment variables. C: `GITHUB_ENV` does not cross into the called workflow either.
notes.explanation: Workflow-level environment variables in the caller are not propagated to the called workflow; inputs are the way to hand it data.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Limitations of reusable workflows”
notes.evidence: Any environment variables set in an `env` context defined at the workflow level in the caller workflow are not propagated to the called workflow.

notes.front: A calling job has `uses:` for a reusable workflow, plus `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` and `needs: build`. Which keyword breaks the rules?
notes.choices:
A) `runs-on`
B) `needs`
C) `uses`
D) None of them
notes.back: A) `runs-on`
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: `needs` and `uses` are on the list of supported keywords. D: `runs-on` is not on it.
notes.explanation: A job that calls a reusable workflow may use only the listed keywords, and `runs-on` is not among them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Supported keywords for jobs that call a reusable workflow”
notes.evidence: When you call a reusable workflow, you can only use the following keywords in the job containing the call: jobs.<job_id>.name jobs.<job_id>.uses jobs.<job_id>.with

notes.front: Your platform team wants a later fix to its build logic to reach every repository without anyone copying files again. Which should it provide?
notes.choices:
A) A workflow template (starter workflow)
B) A reusable workflow that repositories call
C) A `.github` repository with only a `README`
D) A `$default-branch` placeholder
notes.back: B) A reusable workflow that repositories call
notes.choicesExplained: A: a template is copied into a new workflow and is then independent, so later fixes do not reach existing copies. C and D: neither shares build logic.
notes.explanation: A reusable workflow is one central definition that callers invoke through `workflow_call`, whereas a template is a copied scaffold.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Study guide for Exam GH-200: GitHub Actions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: You configure a template that publishes packages, and its workflow reads `${{ secrets.npm_token }}`. What do you do so it can run?
notes.choices:
A) Delete the line, as templates bring their own secrets
B) Store the token as a repository secret named `npm_token`
C) Add `secrets: inherit` to the step
D) Replace it with `$default-branch`
notes.back: B) Store the token as a repository secret named `npm_token`
notes.choicesExplained: A: templates do not supply secret values. C: `inherit` is for calling reusable workflows. D: that placeholder names a branch.
notes.explanation: When a template uses a secret, you store the described value as a secret in your repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using workflow templates”, “Choosing and using a workflow template”
notes.evidence: Some workflow templates use secrets. For example, `${{ secrets.npm_token }}`. If the workflow template uses a secret, store the value described in the secret name as a secret in your repository.

notes.front: In the `.github` repository you add `workflow-templates/lint.yml` and `workflow-templates/lint.json`. The template does not appear as expected. Why?
notes.choices:
A) Templates must be in `.github/workflows`
B) The `.github` repository must be named `templates`
C) The metadata file must be named `lint.properties.json`
D) Templates need `on: workflow_call`
notes.back: C) The metadata file must be named `lint.properties.json`
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: templates belong in the `workflow-templates` directory of the `.github` repository. D: `workflow_call` makes a workflow reusable; it has nothing to do with templates.
notes.explanation: The metadata file takes the workflow file's name with `.properties.json` instead of `.yml`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Metadata file requirements”
notes.evidence: The metadata file must have the same name as the workflow file, but instead of the `.yml` extension, it must be appended with `.properties.json`.

notes.front: Your organisation keeps its templates in a private `.github` repository. A developer creating a workflow in a public repository cannot see them. Why?
notes.choices:
A) Templates appear only after the first workflow run
B) The developer needs write access to `.github`
C) Private `.github` templates are available only to private repositories
D) Public repositories cannot use any templates
notes.back: C) Private `.github` templates are available only to private repositories
notes.choicesExplained: B: the docs speak of granting read access, not write. A: nothing ties templates to earlier runs. D: public repositories can use templates from a public `.github` repository.
notes.explanation: Templates reach only repositories whose visibility matches or is more restricted than the template repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations (reference)”, “Workflow template availability”
notes.evidence: Workflow templates in a private `.github` repository are only available to private repositories.

notes.front: A private repository in your organisation holds a reusable workflow. Another private repository in the same organisation cannot call it. How do you fix this without publishing the workflow?
notes.choices:
A) Make the called repository public
B) Set the called repository's Actions Access setting to allow repositories in the organisation
C) Pin the call to a commit
D) Add `secrets: inherit` to the caller
notes.back: B) Set the called repository's Actions Access setting to allow repositories in the organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A: that publishes the workflow, which the task rules out. D and C: secrets and pinning do not grant access.
notes.explanation: The called workflow's private repository must allow access from the organisation's repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”, “Sharing actions and workflows with your organization”
notes.evidence: To grant access to other private repositories in the organization, in the Access section at the bottom of the page, select Accessible from repositories in the 'ORGANIZATION-NAME' organization

notes.front: On your personal account, a private repository holds a reusable workflow you want to call from your other private repositories without publishing it. What do you do?
notes.choices:
A) Fork it into each repository
B) Copy it into each `.github/workflows` directory
C) In its Actions settings, under Access, allow repositories owned by your user
D) Publish it to GitHub Marketplace
notes.back: C) In its Actions settings, under Access, allow repositories owned by your user
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: copies defeat the point of one shared workflow. D: that publishes it, and reusable workflows cannot be published there anyway.
notes.explanation: The Access setting lets your other private repositories use it without publishing it publicly.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Sharing actions and workflows from your private repository”, “Sharing actions and workflows from your private repository”
notes.evidence: To grant access to other private repositories, in the Access section at the bottom of the page, select Accessible from repositories owned by 'USERNAME' user

notes.front: Some shared steps must run on a different type of machine from the job that needs them. Should you package them as a reusable workflow or as an action that bundles steps (a composite action)?
notes.choices:
A) A reusable workflow, because its jobs specify the machine they run on
B) Either, because both choose their own machine
C) A composite action, because it runs as one step
D) Neither: machines can be set only in the caller
notes.back: A) A reusable workflow, because its jobs specify the machine they run on
notes.choicesExplained: C: a composite action runs inside the calling job, on that job's machine. B: only the reusable workflow has its own jobs. D: a reusable workflow's jobs specify their own machine type.
notes.explanation: The docs say to use a reusable workflow, not a composite action, when the steps need a different machine type.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows versus composite actions”
notes.evidence: Reusable workflows contain one or more jobs. As with all workflow jobs, the jobs in a reusable workflow specify the type of machine on which the job will run.

notes.front: How do reusable workflows and composite actions differ in what they contain and where they run?
notes.back: A reusable workflow can contain several jobs and is called from a job; a composite action holds steps and runs as one step.
notes.explanation: A composite action cannot contain jobs; it runs as a single step within the caller workflow.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows versus composite actions”
notes.evidence: Composite actions contain a series of steps that are run as a single step within the caller workflow. Unlike reusable workflows, they cannot contain jobs.

notes.front: How is logging different for a reusable workflow and a composite action?
notes.back: A reusable workflow logs every job and step separately; a composite action shows as just the one step that ran it.
notes.explanation: The composite action's inner steps do not appear individually in the log.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Reusable workflows versus composite actions”
notes.evidence: When a composite action runs, the log will show just the step in the caller workflow that ran the composite action, not the individual steps within the composite action. With reusable workflows, every job and step is logged separately.

notes.front: According to GitHub's comparison table, which of reusable workflows and composite actions can use secrets?
notes.back: Reusable workflows can use secrets; composite actions cannot.
notes.explanation: The table sets "Can use secrets" against "Cannot use secrets".
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Key differences between reusable workflows and composite actions”
notes.evidence: Can use secrets | Cannot use secrets

notes.front: Which of a reusable workflow and a composite action can be published to GitHub Marketplace?
notes.back: Only the composite action; reusable workflows cannot be published there.
notes.explanation: Sharing a reusable workflow happens through repository access instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Reusing workflow configurations”, “Key differences between reusable workflows and composite actions”
notes.evidence: Cannot be published to the marketplace | Can be published to the marketplace
